questions.question: A number line is drawn from 0 to 12 and cut into 12 equal parts, so there is a tick mark at every whole number: 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on up to 12. Ravi wants to mark √21 on this line. Between which two ticks does √21 land?
options: Between the 4 tick and the 5 tick
Between the 5 tick and the 6 tick
Between the 10 tick and the 11 tick
Between the 3 tick and the 4 tick
questions.explain: Find the perfect squares on each side: 16 < 21 < 25, so √21 sits between √16 = 4 and √25 = 5. Halving (21 ÷ 2 = 10.5) is not the same as taking a square root.

questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 12 with a tick mark at every whole number: 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on up to 12. Sofia has to place √10 on this line. Which statement about √10 is true?
options: Between the 4 tick and the 5 tick
Between the 3 tick and the 4 tick
Right on the 5 tick, since 10 ÷ 2 = 5
Right on a tick, since 10 is a square
questions.explain: Since 9 < 10 < 16, √10 lands between 3 and 4, just past 3. A round number like 10 is not automatically a perfect square, and halving 10 does not give its root.

questions.question: A number line goes from 0 to 10 and is cut into 10 equal parts, so every tick mark is a whole number: 0, 1, 2, and so on up to 10. Which of these square roots lands between the 6 tick and the 7 tick?
questions.explain: The 6 and 7 ticks come from 6 × 6 = 36 and 7 × 7 = 49, so you need a number between 36 and 49, which is 45. The one that says √13 comes from halving 13, and halving is not rooting.

questions.question: A number line stretches from 0 to 16 with a tick mark at every whole number: 0, 1, 2, and so on up to 16. Leo marks √30 between the 5 tick and the 6 tick. Is his placement right?
options: No, it lands on the 15 tick, because 30 ÷ 2 = 15
No, it belongs between 6 and 7, because 30 is near 36
No, it lands right on a tick, because 30 is a square
Yes, because 25 < 30 < 36, so it is past 5
questions.explain: 25 < 30 < 36 means √30 is between √25 = 5 and √36 = 6, so Leo is right. Watch the trap of calling 30 a perfect square just because it looks round.

questions.question: Ella says √72 is between 8 and 9. Which pair of facts proves she is right?
questions.explain: Trap 72 between the perfect squares beside it: 64 < 72 < 81, so √72 is between 8 and 9. Dividing by 2 does not undo squaring.

questions.question: A square patio behind a house in Surrey has an area of 40 square metres. Using mental math, what can you say about the length of one side?
options: Between 5 m and 6 m, since 40 is near 35
Between 6 m and 7 m, since 36 < 40 < 49
Exactly 20 m, since half of 40 is 20
Exactly 6 m, as 40 is a square number
questions.explain: The side is √40, and since 36 < 40 < 49 the side is between 6 m and 7 m. A 20 m side would give an area of 400 square metres, so halving is not rooting.

questions.question: Riya is estimating √90 without a calculator. Which statement is correct?
options: √90 is between 45 and 46, since 90 ÷ 2 = 45
√90 is a whole number, since 90 is a square
√90 is between 9 and 10, since 81 < 90 < 100
√90 is between 10 and 11, since 90 is near 100
questions.explain: 81 < 90 < 100 puts √90 between 9 and 10, close to 9.5. Halving gives 45, but 45 × 45 is 2025, nowhere near 90.

questions.question: A square plot at a community garden in Kelowna has an area of 55 square metres. Which method should you use to estimate the side length in your head?
options: Divide 55 in half, because a root halves it
Divide 55 by 5, because 5 × 5 makes 25
Round 55 to 50 because 50 is a square
Look for the perfect squares around 55
questions.explain: Use the perfect squares just below and just above 55, which are 49 and 64, so the side is between 7 m and 8 m. Rounding to 50 does not help, since 50 is not a perfect square either.

questions.question: A square skateboard pad in a Burnaby park must cover at least 130 square metres, and the sides can only be built in whole metres. What is the smallest whole number of metres each side can be?
questions.explain: Since 121 < 130 < 144, √130 is between 11 and 12, so an 11 m side is too small and 12 m is the smallest whole side that covers 130 square metres. Half of 130 is not its root.

questions.question: A square school garden in Victoria has an area of 60 square metres. Ben wants to put a low fence all the way around it. Which estimate of the perimeter is correct?
options: Between 24 m and 28 m, since a side is 6–7 m
Between 28 m and 32 m, since a side is 7–8 m
Exactly 120 m, since 60 ÷ 2 is 30 per side
Between 32 m and 36 m, since a side is over 8 m
questions.explain: First, 49 < 60 < 64, so one side is between 7 m and 8 m; then multiply by 4 to get a perimeter between 28 m and 32 m. The trap is halving 60 to get a 30 m side.

questions.question: In class Owen says, “To estimate √45, I just take half of 45, so √45 is about 22.5.” What is the best response?
options: He should round 45 to 50, because 50 is a perfect square
Nothing is wrong, because dividing by 2 undoes squaring
Halving is not rooting; 36 < 45 < 49, so √45 is between 6 and 7
He should double 45 first, because 90 is between 81 and 100
questions.explain: Square rooting is the inverse of squaring, not of doubling: 6 × 6 = 36 and 7 × 7 = 49, so √45 sits between 6 and 7. Checking by squaring helps, since 22.5 × 22.5 is over 500.

questions.question: Priya is making a math poster and writes, “50 is a nice round number, so it must be a perfect square, which makes √50 a whole number.” What should her poster say instead?
options: She is right, because round numbers like 50 are always squares
She is wrong; √50 must be 25, because half of 50 is 25
She is wrong; √50 is between 6 and 7, as 6 × 7 = 42
She is wrong; 49 < 50 < 64, so √50 is between 7 and 8
questions.explain: Looking round does not make a number a perfect square: 49 < 50 < 64, so √50 is between 7 and 8 and very close to 7. Squaring your guess is the fast check.
